title: India Can Build Rockets, But Can Its VCs Fund The Next One?
summary: India Can Build Rockets, But Can Its VCs Fund The Next One?

For a country whose space programme was historically dominated by ISRO, it was a powerful demonstration of what Indian entrepreneurs could achieve in advanced technology.

Three months later, Ashlee Vance — the American journalist best known for his bestselling biography of Elon Musk and reporting on the global space industry — turned his attention to India’s technological ambitions.
His question was less about the capabilities of Indian engineers than the willingness of Indian investors to back them.

He asked:
The October 22 post accompanied Vance’s Core Memory feature exploring India’s emerging hardware economy.

After three weeks meeting 15 Indian companies, Vance appeared impressed by the technological ambitions of their founders but far less enthusiastic about the state of the country’s venture capital ecosystem.
He subsequently doubled down, claiming he had rarely encountered a market where VCs had a worse reputation among founders.
Founders complained about investors demanding commercial traction before technologies had been validated, prolonged diligence processes and excessive dependence on founder pedigree.
Investors pushed back, highlighting India’s growing list of deeptech successes, the increasing availability of specialist capital and the structural challenges of financing scientific innovation.
But the timing makes this debate far more consequential than another disagreement on X.

As AI threatens to automate parts of the software-services industry that helped establish India as a global technology powerhouse, the country’s ability to create and own foundational technologies is becoming increasingly important.
India has demonstrated that its entrepreneurs can build complex technologies.
The more difficult question is whether venture capital and private equity can repeatedly back such breakthroughs.
One of the strongest responses came from Akash Kulgod, founder of Dognosis, which is developing canine-assisted cancer detection technology.
In a detailed post , Kulgod compared his experience interacting with approximately 80 investors, around 65% of whom were based in the US.
His criticism ran deeper than simply stating that Indian VCs rejected his startup.
He said US investors typically made relatively quick decisions, rejecting the opportunity when they lacked conviction in the technology or founding team.
Some Indian investors, he alleged, extended discussions over repeated meetings and visits, only to demand commercial traction or stop responding.
For a company developing medical technology, any delays in the development cycle hurt.
Clinical validation, technical testing and regulatory approvals can require years before meaningful commercial revenue becomes possible.
An investor demanding revenue before the technology is proven may effectively eliminate the opportunity instead of properly evaluating the technology.
Kulgod also questioned whether some investors possessed the technical understanding needed to assess unfamiliar scientific problems.
Other founders raised concerns about investor dependence on IIT or IIM credentials, professional networks and the reputations of existing backers when evaluating early-stage startups.
These are undoubtedly individual accounts, not evidence that such practices are universal across Indian VC firms.
But they expose an uncomfortable question.
If investors require commercial traction, institutional validation and another investor’s conviction before writing a cheque, how much technological risk are they actually underwriting?
There is an important difference between financing a technology after it works and financing the experiment that determines whether it can work.
And as the experience of several founders in India shows, the latter remains one of the most difficult investment decisions.
According to Inc42 DataLabs , Indian deeptech startups raised approximately $500 Mn across 87 deals in 2025.
The sector emerged as one of the most active by deal count, but its funding remained substantially below fintech’s $2.5 Bn, enterprise tech’s $1.8 Bn and ecommerce’s $1.7 Bn.
The latest quarterly figures, however, suggest that investor preferences are changing.
In Q3 2026, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 funding deals , compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago quarter.
Funding surged 176% YoY, dramatically outpacing the broader startup ecosystem’s 5% growth.
Deeptech funding nearly tripled, but the number of funded deals actually declined.
Pixxel’s $100 Mn funding round alone accounted for approximately one-third of the deeptech capital deployed during the quarter.
At the broader ecosystem level, investors also wrote larger seed cheques to fewer companies.
Early stage funding fell 18% YoY to $164 Mn across 93 deals, even as the median cheque size increased 20% to $1.2 Mn.
According to Inc42’s H1 2026 funding report , advanced hardware and technology startups raised $365 Mn across a record 66 deals, reflecting an 18% rise in funding and a 53% jump in deal volume.
That suggests improving breadth of investment during the first half, followed by greater concentration in the third quarter.
There’s no trend to explore here, but this disparity demonstrates why headline funding growth is an insufficient measure of access to capital.
Larger investments are increasingly flowing towards a smaller pool of technically validated companies.
So the deeper question is whether more first-time founders pursuing unproven technologies are securing their first institutional cheques, which strikes at the heart of what Vance was saying.
A separate debate over India’s startup funding priorities had already exposed a fundamental divide between founders and investors over where venture capital should flow.

In an October 17 post on X , Neosapien founder Dhananjay Yadav questioned why consumer-service startups burning substantial amounts of capital could attract large investments, while deeptech companies generating higher revenues with lower cash burn struggled to raise even a fraction of that money.

Responding to Yadav, Untitled Ventures’ Anmol Maini made a provocative claim that much of deeptech could eventually prove to be a “grift”, arguing that quick commerce and on-demand services might contribute more to the economy.
Blume Ventures partner Arpit Agarwal offered an explanation rooted in investment economics.
Investment capital, he argued, gravitates towards opportunities offering lower perceived risk or disproportionately higher returns.
The distinction to note here is that the economic importance of a technology and its attractiveness as a venture investment are not necessarily the same thing.

This is consistent with concerns Agarwal had raised in an earlier interview with Inc42 , where he explained why capital-intensive original equipment manufacturing (OEM) businesses are often poorly suited to conventional early-stage VC financing.
Pixxel founder Awais Ahmed, however, challenged the notion that consumer internet and deeptech should be competing for relevance and the same pie of venture capital.
In a detailed post , Ahmed argued that they represent different layers of the same technological economy.

A ten-minute grocery delivery depends on decades of breakthroughs in semiconductors, GPS, lithium-ion batteries, cellular networks and computing — technologies developed long before their commercial applications became apparent.
Consumer businesses make technology accessible at scale.
Deeptech expands what technology can achieve.
Ahmed acknowledged that successful internet companies create wealth that can eventually be reinvested into deeptech.
But foundational technologies cannot simply be treated as investments to pursue once quicker commercial opportunities have been exhausted.
Developing competitive capabilities in semiconductors, aerospace, advanced materials or energy requires years of research, specialised talent, experimentation and industrial infrastructure.
And therein lies India’s venture capital allocation dilemma.
The country has spent the past decade building a thriving consumer internet economy.
But its ambition to emerge as a global technology powerhouse will require investing in foundational technologies long before their commercial returns become predictable.
